system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 4 — Scale Justification Sheets (24)

_Pages 17-41._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## Convergence system definition

> This convergence system shows a fixed bombardment of
> any type chord that we want to give "tonal significance" to then
> bombard it with 24 scales, a mixture of them, their ideas and
> constituent chords.

**Significance (p. 17).** This is the foundational definition of the entire method -- the systematic application of 24 scales to any target chord as a means of approaching tonal resolution.

## Convergence system origin / V-chord technique

> I conceived this convergence system by using a one chord tag
> at the very end of "Stella Bye Starlite." The first chord (numbered)
> of each of the following group of 43 chords & scales yield a different
> type V chord (function) and its parent scale, yielding several con-
> vergent scales & their chords for tonal convergence.

**Significance (p. 21).** Martino explains exactly how the system was conceived -- each of the 43 chords/scales functions as a unique kind of V chord, giving the player dozens of approach routes to a tonal destination.

## Ear preparation before convergence

> Before playing each scale in this
> system, you should brainwash your ear with the
> tonality (F major in this case) with several cadences
> into the key. (Ex. G-7-C7 FA) (G£-C 139 FA)
> I- VI- II- V-T ect.

**Significance (p. 32).** This is a prescriptive practice rule -- the player must first internalize the destination tonality through cadential repetition before attempting convergent scale approaches.

## Aural projection rule

> When converging on a tonality project yourself sound wise to
> it already having your attention (sound attention) on it and
>
> on the chord or scale you are using.

**Significance (p. 34).** This gives the mental/aural technique that accompanies the physical scale work -- the improviser must simultaneously hear the destination while executing the approach scale.

## Scale #1 -- Descending Pentatonic

> Scale #1. A pentatonic scale having a a Dox 7th (of C7 chord)
> in it which resolves voice leadingly into the note
> A (The vital 3rd of F major). Also contains A
> (G-pb ) Tritone which the note pb resolves (as
> both of C 7th) To the 5th (C) and the note G re-
> solves to F the root note.

**Significance (p. 32).** Martino's analysis of Scale #1 establishes the template for all subsequent scale justifications -- each note's convergent function into the target key is traced through tritone and voice-leading logic.

## Scale #4 -- Diminished scale (H-W)

> Scale # 4. This scale is a diminish scale on the tonic "C".
>
> It has an interval structure half, whole, half, whole,
>
> half, whole, half, whole. The scale has an E-B Db tri-
> tone also a G-D ee giving it a number of con-
> vergent factors into major or minor tonality.

**Significance (p. 35).** This is the first diminished scale entry and establishes the H-W interval structure definition used as a reference point for comparing Scale #5.

## Scale #5 -- Diminished scale (W-H)

> Scale # 5.
>
> This scale is a second type diminish scale. It has
>
> a W,H,W,H,W,H,W,H step symmetry. It permits ascending
> diminish color to a point of convergence (F major in
> this case). It has the same symmetrical indifference
> as the # 4 scale which permits it to be used (starting
> on different notes) for converging cadences to several
> tonalities.

**Significance (p. 36).** Distinguishes the W-H diminished scale from the H-W variant and articulates the key property of 'symmetrical indifference' that makes both diminished scales useful across multiple tonal destinations.

## Scale #6 -- Jazz Melodic Minor

> Scale # 6.
>
> This is a Jazz melodic minor scale. It permits a
> minor color-quality asendance into tonality (F major)
> it is important because of its intervallic symmetry
> its D bstarting note, and the different chords it
> produces. (G b oan, E+A7, Be nb7 + pb_4~ 7).

**Significance (p. 37).** Introduces the Jazz melodic minor as a convergent scale type, identifying the characteristic chord it produces and its function as the first of several minor-quality approach scales in the system.

## Scale #7 -- Major scale (#4 & #5)

> Scale # 7.
>
> This scale is a major scale with the 4th degree
> and 5th degree raised. It contains an E bi3 bs
> chord which is the sound of all the scale notes
> sounded together simultaneously.

**Significance (p. 38).** Defines the raised-4th-and-5th major scale type and introduces the technique of stacking all scale tones simultaneously to identify a scale's characteristic chord sound.

## Scale #10 -- Whole Tone scale

> Scale # 10.
>
> This scale is the whole tone scale cb), It has its
> perfect whole, bold steps which leads also into F
> major. The linking chord is the cb7 bs which resolves
> nicely into F major. Other chords which have resolving
> tendencies are the C+7, ¢ 69411, c7b 5.

**Significance (p. 41).** Introduces the whole tone scale as a convergent type, names its characteristic 'linking chord,' and lists the family of chords the scale produces for tonal approach.

## Chord-extraction rule

> Extract all possible chords from all scales for
>
> resolution purposes.

**Significance (p. 34).** This is a direct, universally applicable practice instruction -- every scale in the system should be mined for its constituent chords, each of which can independently serve as a convergent device.

## System purpose -- color and route variety

> Remember this system is about how to get into a major or minor
>
> key variating different scales (24) and chords (many) and their
>
> innumerable permutation & chord inversions.

**Significance (p. 37).** Martino restates the system's core pedagogical goal in a single sentence, clarifying that the 24 scales are not ends in themselves but tools for multiplying approach routes to any tonal destination.
